issues.title: [CI][ROCm] inductor-periodic gfx950 dynamo benchmarks red since ROCm 7.2 -> 7.14 upgrade (#188429)
issues.author: bobrenjc93
issues.body:
TITLE: [CI][ROCm] inductor-periodic gfx950 dynamo benchmarks red since ROCm 7.2 -> 7.14 upgrade (#188429)

LABELS: module: rocm, module: inductor, oncall: pt2, module: ci, high priority

BODY:

`inductor-periodic` has been red on main continuously since 2026-08-08, on the
`rocm-periodic-dynamo-benchmarks-test` (gfx950) jobs. No non-ROCm job in the
workflow is failing. Because the workflow never goes green, it is currently not
able to surface any real inductor regression.

## Root cause

The last green `inductor-periodic` run was `0fc30948e35` (2026-08-07 20:58 UTC).
The first run of the continuous red streak was `7c898a118f0` (2026-08-08 05:03 UTC).

`bb96371605b` -- "[ROCm][CI] Switch rocm-preview to TheRock wheels and upgrade
CI to 7.14 (#188429)" -- landed at 2026-08-07 22:20 UTC, inside that window.

Although the PR title scopes it to `rocm-preview`, it modified
`.ci/docker/common/install_rocm.sh` (+40/-270) and `.ci/docker/ubuntu-rocm/Dockerfile`.
Those are shared image definitions, so the content hash of the
`pytorch-linux-jammy-rocm-n-py3-benchmarks` image changed and *every* ROCm job
picked up the new image, including this periodic benchmark job.

Confirmed by diffing the two runs directly:

| | last green (Aug 7 20:58) | first red (Aug 8 05:03) |
|---|---|---|
| image tag | `...-benchmarks-d233d238439a...` | `...-benchmarks-0c3a9da87a44...` |
| `BUILD_ROCM_VERSION` | `7.2` | `7.14` |
| ROCm root | `/opt/rocm` | `site-packages/_rocm_sdk_devel` (TheRock wheel) |

So this is a ROCm 7.2 -> 7.14 runtime jump on gfx950, not an inductor change.

## Symptoms

Three distinct model/suite failures, stable across 9 consecutive runs
(Aug 8 05:03 through Aug 10 17:02):

1. `torch_multimodal_clip` -- `dynamic_inductor_torchbench` shard 2,
   `accuracy=fail_accuracy, expected=pass`. **9/9 runs, 100% consistent.**
   This is the one that behaves like a genuine numerical change under 7.14.

2. `vit_base_patch14_dinov2.lvd142m` -- `dynamic_inductor_timm` and
   `aot_inductor_timm` shard 2 (inference, `expected=pass`),
   `accuracy=eager_two_runs_differ`. 8/9 runs. Note `eager_two_runs_differ`
   means two *eager* runs disagree -- inductor is not involved at all, the
   model is nondeterministic on this hardware/runtime.

3. `convnextv2_nano.fcmae_ft_in22k_in1k` -- `dynamic_inductor_timm` shard 1
   (training, `expected=fail_accuracy`), reports
   `IMPROVED: accuracy=pass`. 8/9 runs. `check_accuracy.py` exits nonzero on
   improvements too, so a stale pessimistic baseline keeps the job red.
   Overlaps with #189893.

Note: the `EAGER_FAILED` lines in these logs come from `check_graph_breaks.py`
and appear for every model including passing ones. They are not part of the
failure; only `check_accuracy.py` sets the nonzero exit.

## Suggested next steps

- (2) and (3) are baseline/nondeterminism problems and should be rebaselined
  under 7.14 via `benchmarks/dynamo/ci_expected_accuracy/update_expected.py`.
- (1) should be confirmed as an accepted numerical change under ROCm 7.14
  rather than blanket-rebaselined, since it is 100% reproducible and one-directional.
- Longer term, an image-definition change that rebuilds the shared ROCm image
  should probably run the ROCm periodic benchmarks before landing.

back to 2026-08-08. The workflow has not been green for 4 days, so it is
currently incapable of catching any real inductor regression - which is the
actual cost here, beyond the ROCm failures themselves.

Still unassigned after ~18 hours, so tagging people directly.

Restating the root cause from the description, since it is the actionable part:
the failures start in the exact window where `bb96371605b`
("[ROCm][CI] Switch rocm-preview to TheRock wheels and upgrade CI to 7.14",
#188429) landed. Although that PR is scoped to `rocm-preview` by title, it
modified `.ci/docker/common/install_rocm.sh` and `.ci/docker/ubuntu-rocm/Dockerfile`,
which are shared image definitions - so the `pytorch-linux-jammy-rocm-n-py3-benchmarks`
image was rebuilt and *every* ROCm job picked up the new stack, including this one:

|  | last green (Aug 7 20:58) | first red (Aug 8 05:03) |
|---|---|---|
| image tag | `...-benchmarks-d233d238439a...` | `...-benchmarks-0c3a9da87a44...` |
| `BUILD_ROCM_VERSION` | `7.2` | `7.14` |
| ROCm root | `/opt/rocm` | `site-packages/_rocm_sdk_devel` (TheRock wheel) |

Suggested split of the work, since these are not all the same problem:

- `vit_base_patch14_dinov2.lvd142m` reports `eager_two_runs_differ`, i.e. two
  *eager* runs disagree. Inductor is not involved; this is model
  nondeterminism under 7.14 and wants a rebaseline or a flaky-model entry.
- `convnextv2_nano.fcmae_ft_in22k_in1k` is pinned to `fail_accuracy` but now
  passes, so `check_accuracy.py` fails the job on the *improvement*. Stale
  baseline, overlaps #189893.
- `torch_multimodal_clip` is the one I would not rebaseline blindly - it fails
  100% consistently and one-directionally, which looks like a genuine numerical
  change under 7.14 rather than noise.

If a rebaseline under 7.14 is the agreed path for the first two, happy to put
that up; I mainly want confirmation on the third before anyone papers over it.

comments.author: bobrenjc93
comments.body:
@naromero77amd I put up #193216 with the values you specified, ran it against
the real gfx950 jobs, and **the pins do not hold**. Reporting back before
landing since this contradicts the plan we agreed.

Two of the four jobs went green; two stayed red, both the same way:

```
dynamic_inductor_timm 2/2        vit_base_patch14_dinov2  IMPROVED: accuracy=pass, expected=fail_accuracy
dynamic_inductor_torchbench 2/2  torch_multimodal_clip    IMPROVED: accuracy=pass, expected=fail_accuracy
```

Both of those are my errors, not yours -- you were working from what I told you:

- I said `torch_multimodal_clip` failed 100% consistently and one-directionally,
  which is why we agreed on `fail_accuracy`. It **passed** on the very first run
  after being pinned. My 9/9 sample was real but not predictive, so the "looks
  like a genuine numerical change" read is not supported.
- I changed `vit_base_patch14_dinov2` only on the inference baselines, since
  only those were failing, and flagged that as a deliberate deviation from
  "rebase vit with `eager_two_runs_differ`". The untouched **training** baseline
  then went red on an improvement.

The general problem is that `check_accuracy.py` fails a job on a mismatch in
either direction, so for a model that genuinely flips, any pinned value just
selects which outcome turns CI red.

I have switched the PR to add all three to the ROCm-scoped `flaky_models` set
instead, which yields `PASS_BUT_FLAKY`/`FAIL_BUT_FLAKY` and appends to neither
`failed` nor `improved`. That block already carries `alexnet` and `demucs` under
the comment *"Discovered on gfx950 CI after ROCm 7.2 upgrade, eager mode non
determinism"*, which is the same root cause. Simulating every observed outcome
through the real `check_accuracy()`:

```
observed=pass                   job_fails=False
observed=eager_two_runs_differ  job_fails=False
observed=fail_accuracy          job_fails=False
```

Two things I want your call on, since this is your area:

1. This gives up accuracy signal for all three models on ROCm. That matches the
   `alexnet`/`demucs` precedent and your "we will go back and triage later", but
   it does mean a real regression in them would go unnoticed until someone
   revisits.
2. If you would rather keep real signal for `torch_multimodal_clip`, the
   narrower option is extending `get_eager_nondeterministic_models()` to cover
   the ROCm paths -- it currently returns entries only for two CUDA files. That
   tolerates only `pass -> eager_two_runs_differ` and still catches a genuine
   `fail_accuracy`. No existing ROCm precedent for it, but it preserves more
   signal.

Happy to go either way. Keeping this issue open regardless, as you asked.

issues.author: bastefaniak

### 🐛 Describe the bug

When we `torch.compile` function used in `vLLM` during MRoPE computations:
```python
def apply_interleaved_rope(x: torch.Tensor, mrope_section: list[int]) -> torch.Tensor:
    x_t = x[0].clone()
    x_t[..., 1 : mrope_section[1] * 3 : 3] = x[1, ..., 1 : mrope_section[1] * 3 : 3]
    x_t[..., 2 : mrope_section[2] * 3 : 3] = x[2, ..., 2 : mrope_section[2] * 3 : 3]
    return x_t
```

issues.title: [CI][ROCm] convnextv2_nano.fcmae_ft_in22k_in1k flaky accuracy (pass/fail_accuracy) on gfx950 dynamic_inductor_timm training
issues.author: bobrenjc93
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`convnextv2_nano.fcmae_ft_in22k_in1k` flakes between `pass` and `fail_accuracy`
across runs on the ROCm (gfx950) periodic timm **training** job, reding the whole
shard on the runs where it fails:

```
convnextv2_nano.fcmae_ft_in22k_in1k  FAIL:  accuracy=fail_accuracy, expected=pass
```

**Job:** `inductor-periodic / rocm-periodic-dynamo-benchmarks-test / test (dynamic_inductor_timm, 1, 2, linux.rocm.gpu.gfx950.1)`

It is **not deterministic**. Recent scheduled `inductor-periodic` runs:

- PASS (whole shard green): run 28761777577 (2026-07-06), run 29141468015 (2026-07-11)
- FAIL (`fail_accuracy`): runs 29153750595, 29216980590, 29227342978, 29240693239,
  29253925514, 29270323000, 29284973629, 29297829175, 29308942309, 29321479172,
  29335258201, and others (2026-07-11 .. 2026-07-14)

### Root cause

Appears to be a gfx950 / ROCm 7.2 numerics issue rather than a PyTorch/inductor
regression: `convnextv2_nano` **passes on CUDA (a10g)** in the same runs and passes
in the ROCm *eval* config; only ROCm gfx950 *training* flakes. This is the same
class as the alexnet/demucs "gfx950 CI after ROCm 7.2 upgrade, eager mode
non determinism" entries already in `check_accuracy.py`.

### Fix / mitigation

Because it is flaky, freezing `fail_accuracy` into the expected CSV would re-red the
job on the runs where it flakes back to `pass` (`check_accuracy.py` treats a
pass-when-baseline-is-fail as an "improvement" and exits non-zero). So instead it is
added to the ROCm `flaky_models` set in `benchmarks/dynamo/check_accuracy.py`, which
tolerates both `pass` and `fail_accuracy`. See PR #189880.

This issue tracks root-causing and removing the flaky-list entry once the gfx950
divergence is understood/fixed.

### Versions

ROCm 7.2, gfx950 CI (pytorch-linux-jammy-rocm-n-py3-benchmarks image).

issues.title: [Inductor][AOTI][B200] TorchBench compilation latency regressed 57% since Aug 11
issues.author: bobrenjc93
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

The compiler performance dashboard shows a sustained AOTInductor compilation-latency regression for TorchBench bfloat16 inference on B200:

| Date | Workflow / commit | Geomean compilation latency |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Aug 11 | [31468859815](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/31468859815) / `b2329090622d` | 19.76 s |
| Aug 12 | [31574146715](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/31574146715) / `1394bc6924ad` | 25.52 s (+29.1%) |
| Aug 13 | [31677954602](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/31677954602) / `04a7716a37e2` | 30.96 s (+21.3% day/day, +56.7% vs Aug 11) |

This is above the dashboard's 15% compilation-latency regression threshold on both days.

This is not caused by a changing model cohort: all three AOTInductor reports contain the same 43 models. Comparing Aug 11 to Aug 13, 21/43 models are more than 15% slower and the median model ratio is 1.147. Several models have much larger changes:

| Model | Aug 11 | Aug 13 | Ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `basic_gnn_edgecnn` | 7.00 s | 50.16 s | 7.17x |
| `shufflenet_v2_x1_0` | 13.51 s | 75.74 s | 5.61x |
| `mnasnet1_0` | 11.51 s | 51.87 s | 4.51x |
| `phlippe_densenet` | 12.88 s | 56.67 s | 4.40x |
| `functorch_dp_cifar10` | 10.45 s | 45.25 s | 4.33x |
| `densenet121` | 27.86 s | 110.09 s | 3.95x |

The spikes are not uniform: some models spiked on Aug 12 and recovered on Aug 13, while others first spiked on Aug 13. This may be B200 AOTI-specific resource contention or flakiness rather than a single deterministic code regression, but the aggregate has remained above the prior baseline for two consecutive runs.

Cross-checks make the signal look specific to B200 AOTInductor:

- AOTInductor TorchBench bfloat16 inference stayed stable over Aug 12 → Aug 13 on A100 (32.85 → 32.93 s), H100 (26.95 → 27.02 s), and MI355X (15.42 → 14.90 s).
- Other B200 compiler modes stayed stable over Aug 11 → Aug 12 → Aug 13: default (9.69 → 9.63 → 9.71 s), cudagraphs (7.97 → 7.89 → 7.84 s), and cpp_wrapper (13.55 → 13.50 → 13.59 s).
- The Aug 13 workflow as a whole failed because other jobs had runner/container infrastructure failures, but the [TorchBench benchmark job](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/31677954602/job/94382983210) succeeded and uploaded a complete 43-model AOTInductor report.

The first observed bad range is `b2329090622d..1394bc6924ad` (Aug 11 to Aug 12). A repeat on a clean B200 runner would help distinguish runner noise from a code regression before bisecting that range.

### Versions

PyTorch main, B200 CUDA benchmark runners, bfloat16 inference, TorchBench AOTInductor.

issues.title: [Inductor][CPU] torch.compile changes int8 batched matmul output dtype to int64
issues.author: lackjava-creator
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

 I am filing it because the minimized case shows an Inductor-only dtype contract violation on both the 2.13 release and the latest nightly.

>
> On CPU, `torch.compile(..., backend="inductor")` changes the output dtype of some same-dtype `int8` batched matrix multiplications from `torch.int8` to `torch.int64`. Native eager, the `eager` backend, and `aot_eager` all return `torch.int8`.
>
> The numerical values happen to match in this small example, but the output dtype does not. This can change downstream type promotion and dispatch.
>
> Minimal self-contained reproducer:
>
> ```python
> import torch
>
> def model(a, b):
>     return torch.matmul(a, b)
>
> a = torch.ones((1, 1, 2), dtype=torch.int8)
> b = torch.ones((1, 2, 2), dtype=torch.int8)
>
> eager = model(a, b)
> compiled = torch.compile(
>     model,
>     backend="inductor",
>     fullgraph=True,
>     dynamic=False,
> )(a, b)
>
> print("torch:", torch.__version__)
> print("git:", torch.version.git_version)
> print("eager:", eager, eager.dtype)
> print("compiled:", compiled, compiled.dtype)
>
> assert compiled.dtype == eager.dtype
> ```
>
> Output on the latest nightly:
>
> ```text
> torch: 2.14.0.dev20260727
> git: ee6a51f8364b126e4e3a3d4459f8fbb35d6a5d3a
> eager:    tensor([[[2, 2]]], dtype=torch.int8)  torch.int8
> compiled: tensor([[[2, 2]]])                    torch.int64
> AssertionError
> ```
>
> The same reproducer also fails on PyTorch `2.13.0`, git commit `cf30153c4c131c8164ee7798e5022d810682e2cb`.
>
> Backend/settings ablation on `2.14.0.dev20260727`:
>
> | Execution | `dynamic=False` | `dynamic=True` |
> |---|---|---|
> | native eager | `torch.int8` | `torch.int8` |
> | `backend="eager"` | `torch.int8` | `torch.int8` |
> | `backend="aot_eager"` | `torch.int8` | `torch.int8` |
> | `backend="inductor"` | **`torch.int64`** | **`torch.int64`** |
>
> `torch.bmm` shows the same behavior. Contiguous and non-contiguous inputs both reproduce it. Three additional independent processes with fresh `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` values reproduced it 3/3.
>
> Shape boundary observed during minimization:
>
> - Affected examples include `(1,1,2) @ (1,2,2)`, `(1,2,2) @ (1,2,1)`, and `(2,2,3) @ (2,3,1)`.
> - Tested 2-D `mm` shapes return the correct `torch.int8` dtype.
> - Some 3-D square or degenerate shapes also return the correct dtype, so rank 3 alone is not sufficient.
>
> This is an integer dtype comparison: no floating-point tolerance is involved, no max/min indices are compared, and the reproducer contains no randomness.
>
> I did not find an exact duplicate. The closest reports I found were #177629, #177630, and #172183, but those concern mixed floating dtypes where eager raises while compiled execution succeeds. #144362 is a broader dtype-check tracker.

My assessment is that this is a correctness issue even though the small example's values match, because compiled execution should preserve eager's output dtype and downstream behavior can depend on it. The quoted technical section above was prepared with Codex assistance; the experiment and decision to report the reproduced dtype violation are mine.

### Error logs

> No compiler exception is raised. The failure is the explicit dtype assertion:
>
> ```text
> eager dtype:    torch.int8
> compiled dtype: torch.int64
> AssertionError
> ```

issues.author: rmcgibbo
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Here's a bit of code that crashes that I think ought to be allowed.

I believe the issue is that the coordination between the `all_reduce` and the `wait_tensor` is handled in ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp by creating a CUDA event ([around here](https://sourcegraph.com/r/github.com/pytorch/pytorch@62885a375afb5fee9898ec8e5c9e41ec37ec1c01/-/blob/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp?L582-584)), and this event isn't created with `cudaEventExternal`. This means that when the event creation is captured in a cudagraph, we can't wait on the event from eager code or from a subsequent cudagraph. So if a graph break gets inserted between the collective and the wait, things work fine under modes that don't use cudagraphs but break with cudagraphs.

import os

import torch
import torch.distributed as dist

dist.init_process_group("nccl")
torch.cuda.set_device(int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"]))

    pending = torch.ops._c10d_functional.all_reduce.default(x, "sum", group)
    torch._dynamo.graph_break()
    return torch.ops._c10d_functional.wait_tensor.default(pending)

x = torch.ones(16, device="cuda")
for _ in range(3):

dist.destroy_process_group()

issues.title: torch.compile cannot pass symbolic stride tuples to Triton kernels
issues.author: drisspg
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug
### Human

Another one that is pretty similar to https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/192288

I probs just encourage using custom ops from the get go and not trying UDF triton kernels


### AGENT Note

A direct Triton kernel launch works eagerly when `x.stride()` is passed as a constexpr tuple, but
`torch.compile(fullgraph=True, dynamic=True)` rejects the same launch with:

```text
Unexpected argument type for a Triton kernel: TupleVariable(length=2)
```

Passing each stride as a separate constexpr argument works. Wrapping the launcher in an opaque
`torch.library.custom_op` also works because `x.stride()` is then evaluated at runtime outside
Dynamo. It would be useful for direct Triton integration to accept tuples of symbolic strides, or to
document the intended compiler-visible representation for a shape/stride tuple.

### Minimal reproduction

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def copy_2d_kernel(
    x,
    output,
    rows: tl.constexpr,
    cols: tl.constexpr,
    X_STRIDES: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK: tl.constexpr,
):
    offsets = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    row = offsets // cols
    col = offsets % cols
    mask = offsets < rows * cols
    values = tl.load(x + row * X_STRIDES[0] + col * X_STRIDES[1], mask=mask)
    tl.store(output + offsets, values, mask=mask)


def copy_2d(x):
    output = torch.empty(x.numel(), dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device)
    copy_2d_kernel[(triton.cdiv(x.numel(), 256),)](
        x,
        output,
        rows=x.shape[0],
        cols=x.shape[1],
        X_STRIDES=x.stride(),
        BLOCK=256,
    )
    return output.view(x.shape)


x = torch.randn(8, 16, device="cuda").T
expected = x.contiguous()
actual = torch.compile(copy_2d, fullgraph=True, dynamic=True)(x)
torch.testing.assert_close(actual, expected)
```

The launch succeeds without `torch.compile`. Under `torch.compile`, it fails while tracing the
kernel call:

```text
torch._dynamo.exc.Unsupported: triton kernel unsupported feature
  Explanation: Encountered triton kernel unsupported feature: Unexpected argument type for a Triton kernel: TupleVariable(length=2).

from user code:
  File "repro.py", line 26, in copy_2d
    copy_2d_kernel[...](...)
```

### Expected behavior

`torch.compile` should accept the tuple of symbolic strides and pass it to the Triton constexpr
argument, consistent with eager execution. Alternatively, there should be a compiler-visible tuple
representation that avoids splitting every shape and stride into a separate kernel parameter.

### Workarounds

Both of these work:

1. Pass `x.stride(0)` and `x.stride(1)` as separate Triton constexpr arguments and reconstruct the
   tuple inside the kernel.
2. Put the launcher behind `torch.library.custom_op`, register a fake implementation, and pass
   `x.stride()` from the opaque runtime implementation.

### Environment

```text
torch: 2.14.0.dev20260811+cu132
torch git: 50e2fa0ee83b69c86861f0c6835977e10dbb111b
triton: 3.8.0
CUDA: 13.2
GPU: NVIDIA GB300
```

issues.title: [inductor] torch.compile fails to compile cumsum on a 0-dim constant tensor: IndexError: tuple index out of range (0-dim variant of #179571, persists on torch 2.12.0)
issues.author: BUAA-Wander
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

This is a 0-dim variant of the previously reported #179571 (`torch.compile` raises an error for constant-tensor `cumsum` patterns while eager mode succeeds), which was closed because maintainers could not reproduce it. It **still reproduces on the released torch 2.12.0+cu130** with a much smaller reproducer. This report adds a minimal reproducer, a backend ablation, and the full traceback.

`torch.compile` with the default `inductor` backend fails at compile time with `IndexError: tuple index out of range` when the graph contains `cumsum` applied to a 0-dimensional (scalar) constant tensor. The same code runs fine in eager mode.

Minimal reproducer:

```python
import torch

def f():
    return torch.tensor(5.0).cumsum(0)

print(f())                  # tensor(5.)
print(torch.compile(f)())   # InductorError: IndexError: tuple index out of range
```

Ablation:

- Also crashes for `torch.tensor(5).cumsum(0)`, `torch.tensor(True).cumsum(0)`, `torch.zeros(()).cumsum(0)`, `torch.full((), 5.0).cumsum(0)`, and `cumsum(-1)`.
- `aot_eager` and `eager` backends compile and run fine, so the failure is specific to the `inductor` backend.
- Runtime-produced 0-dim tensors (`torch.rand(())`, `torch.ones(4).sum()`) do **not** crash; 1-dim constant tensors (`torch.tensor([5.0])`) do **not** crash.
- The failure is in inductor's `pointless_cumsum_replacement` pattern: it computes `dim_size = shape[dim]` on the empty shape tuple of the 0-dim tensor (`torch/_inductor/fx_passes/post_grad.py:923`).

Expected behavior: compilation succeeds and the compiled function returns `tensor(5.)`, matching eager.

comments.author: Juanpacol
comments.body:
Hi all,

I looked into this issue (with the help of an AI coding assistant) and opened a fix here: #191635.

> The following analysis and fix summary were produced with AI assistance and reviewed by me before posting.

There are 3 separate gaps, all reducing to the same missing dispatch mechanism ("split `args[0]` off as `self`, dispatch the rest to `args[0].call_method(...)`"), which already existed elsewhere in Dynamo but wasn't applied consistently:

1. `MyType.__eq__(i, i)` — comparison dunders resolve to a `GetAttrVariable` bound to the class, which forwards *both* operands into `call_method`. That hits the generic richcompare path, which assumes bound-call semantics (exactly one "other" argument) and raises a spurious `TypeError` → `ObservedException`.
2. `MyType.__sizeof__(...)` — `UserDefinedClassVariable.call_method` only special-cases a curated allowlist of `object`-inherited methods, with no entry for `__sizeof__` (and even the bound form `obj.__sizeof__()` wasn't implemented anywhere).
3. `list.__len__` / `list.append` — `list` is modeled by `ListBuiltinVariable`, which never got the generic unbound-method fallback that `DictBuiltinVariable` already has (why `dict.get(d, "b")` already works today).

PR #191635 adds the missing dispatch cases, reusing the existing pattern rather than a new abstraction. I verified the exact reproducer above now matches eager output for all four calls.

Note: `tuple`/`str`/`set`/`frozenset` are modeled by the generic `BuiltinVariable` and likely share the same latent gap — left as a follow-up, out of scope for this fix.

Thanks for the clear repro, it made this straightforward to track down!

issues.title: Nested nested_compile_region silently reuses a body specialized on the inner region's guards
issues.author: aperson30
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

An outer `nested_compile_region` can reuse a cached body that was specialized on a guard collected while tracing an *inner* region. The outer region's reuse condition never sees that guard, so it reuses a body traced under a branch the current call does not take, and the result is silently wrong. No indexing is involved.

```python
import torch

ncr = torch.compiler.nested_compile_region


class Layer(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, flag):
        super().__init__()
        self.flag = flag


@ncr
def inner(layer, x):
    if layer.flag:          # guard lands in the INNER region's trace
        return x.sin()
    return x.cos()


@ncr
def outer(layer, x):
    return inner(layer, x) + 1.0


layers = [Layer(True), Layer(False), Layer(True), Layer(False)]


def fn(x):
    return sum(outer(l, x) for l in layers)


x = torch.randn(8)
print(fn(x))
print(torch.compile(fn, backend="aot_eager", fullgraph=True)(x))
```

### Actual vs expected

```
eager   : [5.8224, 5.6067, 5.9738]
compiled: [3.6594, 3.2790, 3.9479]
```

Two speculate calls instead of four: the `flag=False` layers reuse the `flag=True` body, so every layer computes `sin`.

`SubgraphTracer.traced_sources` is per tracer and does not propagate outward, so `build_reuse_condition` for the outer region collects no guard for `layer.flag` even though the inner trace installed one.

Found while working on #191781 item 3, but unrelated to it: this needs no indexing and reproduces on a clean checkout.

issues.title: dynamo: `AssertionError: lift_tracked_freevar_to_input should not be called on root SubgraphTracer` — dynamic shapes × non-reentrant checkpoint with conditional cross-attention
issues.author: rwightman
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Summary

As with #193193, I encountered this while working on OpenCLIP enhancements. With dynamic enabled for torch.compile I encounter a hard crash involving torch.compile w/ dynamic shapes with MaMMUT style models that involve multiple traversal of the same block w/ cross attention active. Claude assisted analysis below.

A transformer training step whose blocks are wrapped in
`torch.utils.checkpoint(use_reentrant=False)` crashes hard under dynamic shapes when the step
has this (CoCa/MaMMUT-style) structure: blocks carry a cross-attention sublayer that is active
only when a context tensor is passed, and the step traverses the same blocks twice — once with
`context=None`, once with a context tensor. With `torch.compile(dynamic=True)` (or
automatic-dynamic's second-shape recompile on variable-length batches), dynamo asserts while
tracing the checkpoint HOP body:

```
AssertionError: lift_tracked_freevar_to_input should not be called on root SubgraphTracer
```

(a free symbolic size created outside the checkpoint subgraph fails to lift into it). Identical
assertion on **2.9.1+cu130 and 2.13.0+cu130**. The crash is mid-training in real workloads:
automatic-dynamic triggers it on the second distinct batch shape.

### Repro

`pt_ckpt_compile_repro.py` (attached, self-contained, no third-party deps): 12 pre-norm blocks
(RMSNorm / SDPA / gated attn / qk-norm / SwiGLU), a cross-attention sublayer on every 2nd block
(active only when a context is passed), per-block non-reentrant checkpoint, bf16 autocast.
`--dynamic` compiles with `dynamic=True` and feeds two sequence lengths; `--dual` enables the
second (context-free) traversal.

```
python pt_ckpt_compile_repro.py --dynamic --xattn --dual   # crashes on 2.9.1 and 2.13.0
python pt_ckpt_compile_repro.py --dynamic                  # plain stack: no crash
```

The conditional-cross-attention + dual-traversal structure is required: a plain checkpointed
stack compiles fine under `dynamic=True` on both versions, including with RoPE tensors and
boolean SDPA masks passed into the checkpointed blocks.

On a full model with this structure (open_clip MaMMUT2), 2.9.1 sometimes fails later instead,
in inductor (`BackendCompilerFailed: AssertionError: -190873324687087/200000000000000`, an
assert on a SymPy rational during codegen) — depending on model detail this combination dies in
dynamo or in inductor, but it always dies.

### Expected

Either successful symbolic compilation, or a graceful fallback (skip frame / specialize) —
never a hard crash mid-training.

### Notes

- Workaround: `torch._dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = False` (pure per-shape
  specialization) works on both versions, combined with padding sequence lengths to a multiple
  to bound the shape set.

issues.title: `torch.compile` silently computes wrong gradients for chained modulated LayerNorms with a shared scale/shift parameter (regression 2.9.1 → 2.10.0 due to mix_order_reduction)
issues.author: Lakonik
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When a model applies two chained "modulated norm" blocks of the form `x = x + (layer_norm(x) * (1 + scale) + shift)`, where all `scale`/`shift` vectors are **chunks of one shared parameter** (the DiT / AdaLN `scale_shift_table` pattern used by Wan 2.1), the Inductor-compiled backward produces **silently wrong gradients for the second norm's `shift`/`scale` slices** once the total reduction size `batch*seq` is large (≳16k tokens). The first norm's slices are correct to fp32 precision; the second norm's slices come back with relative errors of up to ~1e+6 — depending on graph arrangement the corresponding region of the grad buffer is simply never written, so it can also surface as bitwise-stale values from a previous backward.

**Update: This is a regression introduced in 2.10.0**: the same script is fully clean on 2.9.1 and fails identically on 2.10.0, 2.11.0, and 2.13.0 (latest stable).

Minimal repro in plain fp32, plain `nn.LayerNorm`, no autocast, no checkpointing, no attention:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

DIM, SEQ, SMALL_SEQ = 1024, 32768, 4096
dev = 'cuda'


def run(seq=SEQ, n_norms=2, slicing='chunk'):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    norms = [nn.LayerNorm(DIM, 1e-6, elementwise_affine=False).to(dev)
             for _ in range(n_norms)]
    if slicing == 'separate':
        params = [nn.Parameter(torch.randn(DIM, device=dev) / DIM ** 0.5)
                  for _ in range(2 * n_norms)]
    else:
        table = nn.Parameter(
            torch.randn(1, 2 * n_norms, DIM, device=dev) / DIM ** 0.5)
        params = [table]

    def fn(x):
        if slicing == 'separate':
            mods = params
        elif slicing == 'unbind':
            mods = [s.unsqueeze(1) for s in params[0].unbind(1)]
        else:  # 'chunk' — the failing case
            mods = params[0].chunk(2 * n_norms, dim=1)
        for i, norm in enumerate(norms):
            shift, scale = mods[2 * i], mods[2 * i + 1]
            x = x + (norm(x) * (1 + scale) + shift)
        return x.square().mean()

    fn_c = torch.compile(fn, mode='default', dynamic=False)
    x = torch.randn(1, seq, DIM, device=dev)

    def grads():
        g = [p.grad for p in params]
        for p in params:
            p.grad = None
        return torch.cat([t.reshape(-1) for t in g])

    fn(x).backward()
    g_eager = grads()
    fn_c(x).backward()
    g_compiled = grads()

    rel = ((g_eager - g_compiled).abs().max()
           / g_eager.abs().max().clamp(min=1e-12)).item()
    return rel


CASES = [
    ('chunked table, 2 norms, seq 32768  (THE BUG)', dict()),
    ('same but seq 4096', dict(seq=SMALL_SEQ)),
    ('same but single norm', dict(n_norms=1)),
    ('same but unbind(1)+unsqueeze(1) instead of chunk', dict(slicing='unbind')),
    ('same but 4 independent parameters', dict(slicing='separate')),
]

for name, kwargs in CASES:
    rel = run(**kwargs)
    print(f'{"FAIL" if rel > 0.1 else "ok  "}  max rel grad err {rel:9.3e}  {name}',
          flush=True)

print('\nexpected: first row FAIL (silently wrong grads), all others ok')
```

### Output

On H100 — **identical on torch 2.10.0, 2.11.0 and 2.13.0** (cu126/cu128/cu129 builds all affected; CUDA toolkit version is irrelevant). **torch 2.9.1 is clean** (first row `ok  2.141e-07`):

```
FAIL  max rel grad err 1.481e+06  chunked table, 2 norms, seq 32768  (THE BUG)
ok    max rel grad err 2.068e-07  same but seq 4096
ok    max rel grad err 2.251e-07  same but single norm
ok    max rel grad err 2.141e-07  same but unbind(1)+unsqueeze(1) instead of chunk
ok    max rel grad err 2.116e-07  same but 4 independent parameters
```

### What we bisected (each ingredient is necessary)

1. **Two chained modulated norms** — a single one is clean.
2. **Gradient flow through a multiplicative rsqrt-variance statistic** — an RMSNorm-style `x * rsqrt(mean(x^2) + eps)` fails exactly like LayerNorm; removing the norm, subtracting only the mean (`x - x.mean(-1, keepdim=True)`), or detaching the norm statistics (same forward, pointwise backward) are all clean.
3. **The modulation vectors must be `chunk`/narrow slices of one shared tensor** — `unbind(1)` (+`unsqueeze(1)` for the broadcast shape) or independent parameters are clean. The shared tensor need not be a parameter: chunking a conditioning MLP's output fails the same way (max rel err 7.2e+1 / 4.7e+5 on 2.11 / 2.13, landing in the MLP weight grads). In every failing case the slice grads assemble into one buffer — matching the never-written/stale-buffer behavior.
4. **The slices must broadcast over batch AND sequence, with total `batch*seq` ≳ 16k** — at DIM=5120: seq 8192 ok, seq 16384 FAIL; also FAIL at DIM=256 with long seq, and at batch 8 × seq 4096 (shared table) even though batch 1 × seq 4096 is ok. Per-sample modulation (a real batch dim, e.g. `lin(c).view(B, 4, D)` with B ≥ 2) is clean at every tested length (B=2 × seq 32768, B=4 × seq 65536 ok) — but at B=1 it degenerates to the broadcast case and fails (B=1 × seq 32768 FAIL). Note the two roles of batch size: within the broadcast case it only contributes to the total (B=8 × 4096 fails like B=1 × 32768), while B ≥ 2 per-sample modulation is clean even with a 65536-long reduction per grad element — so the broadcast structure selects the buggy codegen path, and reduction size is the trigger only within it.

Not required: autocast/bf16, gradient checkpointing, attention/FFN, `elementwise_affine`. No escape via compile config (`default`/`reduce-overhead`/`max-autotune`, `fullgraph` on/off, `dynamic` on/off), `TORCHINDUCTOR_SPLIT_REDUCTIONS=0`, or expression rewrites (cloning the norm output or slices, `contiguous()`, `torch.addcmul`, distributing the multiply) — only the `unbind`/separate-parameter rewrites, which change how the slice grads are routed, avoid it.

### Real-world impact

Found while training diffusers Wan 2.1 14B (video diffusion): the per-block `scale_shift_table` gradients were garbage, and since the grad-buffer region is never written, iteration N reused iteration N-1's values bitwise whenever shapes matched — a linearly growing grad-norm staircase.

Who is exposed: any chained-modulated-norm model whose modulation slices broadcast over the batch — learnable scale-shift tables (Wan-style, at any batch size), or ordinary per-sample adaLN whenever the local batch is 1 (common in long-video training and gradient accumulation). Per-sample adaLN at local batch ≥ 2 tested clean at every length (up to seq 65536), and we verified three real DiT-family ImageNet training configs are unaffected.

### Versions

Fails on 2.10.0+cu128, 2.11.0+cu128/cu129, 2.13.0+cu126/cu129; clean on 2.9.1+cu128 (regression window: 2.9.1 → 2.10.0). `collect_env` for the primary environment:

```
PyTorch version: 2.13.0+cu129
Is debug build: False
CUDA used to build PyTorch: 12.9
OS: Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (x86_64)
GCC version: (Ubuntu 11.4.0-1ubuntu1~22.04.3) 11.4.0
Libc version: glibc-2.35
Python version: 3.11.10 (64-bit runtime)
Python platform: Linux-5.15.0-131-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.35
Is CUDA available: True
CUDA runtime version: 12.9.86
GPU models and configuration: 8x NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3
Nvidia driver version: 550.127.08
cuDNN version: 9.10.2
triton: 3.7.1
```

### A related observation

On 2.11.0 only, the same setup with independent parameters of shape `[1, 1, D]` (instead of `[D]` used above) made the compiled backward crash outright (`Function CompiledFunctionBackward returned an invalid gradient at index 3 - got [1024] but expected shape compatible with [1, 1, 1024]`). 2.13.0 neither crashes nor miscomputes there — so the grad-shape handling in this area changed between 2.11 and 2.13 while the silent bug above survived; possibly a useful hint for locating it.

### AI assistance disclosure

Per the [PyTorch AI policy](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/AI_POLICY.md):
The bug was hit in a real training run (Wan 2.1 14B). The debugging, ablation, and this write-up were developed with AI assistance (Claude Fable 5). Every number and code path in this report was executed and verified on our cluster (H100, both torch versions), and I have reviewed and can speak to all of it.

comments.author: primecai
comments.body:
Root cause may be the **mix-order reduction** path, present and default-enabled in OSS from
2.10: `torch._inductor.config.triton.mix_order_reduction` is absent in 2.9.1 and defaults to
on in 2.10.0, matching the observed regression window.

Workaround, with `torch.compile` still enabled:

```bash
TORCHINDUCTOR_MIX_ORDER_REDUCTION=0
```

Verified to restore eager agreement (max relative error ≈ 2e-7) on 2.10.0 and 2.11.0 / H200 at
seq=32768/dim=1024, seq=16384/dim=5120 and batch=8/seq=4096/dim=1024.

In the generated backward, the four gradient slices of the `[1, 4, D]` modulation table should
each be a `reinterpret_tensor` view into one buffer. 2.9.1 emits all four; 2.10.0 emits only
the first two, and the missing two are exactly the second norm's `c_shift` / `c_scale`. In the
mix-order path those two are materialized as standalone tensors out of the reduction
workspace and have no consumer, so their regions of the returned `empty_strided` buffer keep
unspecified contents.

comments.author: haojiang01
comments.body:
Thanks for the excellent diagnosis — the bisect to 2.10 and the observation that the second norm's slices are "materialized as standalone tensors out of the reduction workspace with no consumer" pointed straight at the root cause.

Confirmed: in `_codegen_mix_order_reduction`, the final-reduce step emits `buf = workspace[...].sum(dim=0)`, which rebinds the Python variable. When the reduction output is a view into a shared buffer (`NonOwningLayout`, here the `cat` assembling the chunked table's grad slices), the `reinterpret_tensor` alias is discarded and that region of the grad buffer is never written — hence the uninitialized/bitwise-stale values.

Fix in #193103: write through the view with `copy_()` instead of rebinding. Verified against the repro here plus the batch-8, dim-5120, and chunked-MLP-output ablations. Until it lands, `TORCHINDUCTOR_MIX_ORDER_REDUCTION=0` remains the correct workaround.

issues.title: dynamo=True export: F.linear with 1D weight emits MatMul whose value_info rank doesn't match the emitted graph
issues.author: gabrielfruet
issues.body:
## Bug description

`F.linear(input, weight)` with a 1D `weight` (shape `(in_features,)`, no `bias`) does a per-row dot product in eager PyTorch, dropping the last dim: output shape is `input.shape[:-1]`.

`torch.onnx.export(..., dynamo=True)` lowers this to an ONNX `MatMul` against the weight reshaped to `(in_features, 1)`. That's a valid lowering — ONNX `MatMul` has no 1D-weight special case — and the *actual* node output is rank 2 (`(..., 1)`). But the exporter records `value_info` for that output using the original rank-1 PyTorch shape, not the rank-2 shape the graph it just emitted actually produces.

`onnx.checker.check_model(model, full_check=True)` catches the inconsistency:

```
[ShapeInferenceError] Inference error(s): (op_type:MatMul, node name: node_linear):
[ShapeInferenceError] Inferred shape and existing shape differ in rank: (2) vs (1)
```

ONNX Runtime doesn't use the stale `value_info` and runs fine, so this only surfaces under strict checking (`full_check=True`) or consumers that trust the shape annotation.

## Reproduction

```python
import onnx
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torch.nn as nn


class Integral(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x, project):
        # x: (batch, 300, 4, 33)
        shape = x.shape
        x = F.softmax(x.reshape(-1, 33), dim=1)  # (batch*300*4, 33)
        x = F.linear(x, project)  # project: (33,) -> x: (batch*300*4,), rank drops by 1

    m, (x, project), "model.onnx",
    dynamo=True,
    dynamic_shapes={"x": {0: torch.export.Dim("batch")}, "project": None},
)

issues.title: [ONNX] Dynamo export freezes dynamic time dimension in manual bidirectional LSTM/GRU pattern
issues.author: SouperDuper
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.onnx.export(..., dynamo=True)` exports a manual bidirectional LSTM or GRU pattern with a dynamic time axis, but the generated ONNX graph contains the example input time length in an internal `Expand` shape.

The exported model runs in ONNX Runtime for the example length, then fails for a different valid time length.

The same pattern works with `torch.onnx.export(..., dynamo=False)`.

The control cases in the full reproducer show that these related cases work with `dynamo=True`:

- bare unidirectional `nn.LSTM`
- bare unidirectional `nn.GRU`
- masked unidirectional `nn.LSTM`
- masked unidirectional `nn.GRU`

The clean reproduction environment used the CUDA 13.0 PyTorch wheel, but the reproducer itself executes entirely on CPU and uses ONNX Runtime's `CPUExecutionProvider`.

### Reproduction

Full reproducer (script + requirements.txt): https://gist.github.com/SouperDuper/d00d4e94e4461f9fc3c08bf7815d32fe

The full reproducer above imports only PyTorch, ONNX, ONNX Script, ONNX Runtime, NumPy, and standard-library modules. It adds LSTM and GRU control cases, compares the legacy exporter, and inspects the generated graph for literal Expand dimensions.

The slightly smaller reproducer below shows narrower failing case plus the `dynamo=False` comparison.

Run: `python filename.py`

```python
from __future__ import annotations

import tempfile
import logging
from contextlib import redirect_stderr, redirect_stdout
from io import StringIO
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import onnxruntime as ort
import torch


logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)

def reverse_valid_prefix(
    x: torch.Tensor,
    key_padding_mask: torch.Tensor,
) -> torch.Tensor:
    lengths = (~key_padding_mask).to(dtype=torch.long).sum(dim=1)
    positions = torch.ones_like(key_padding_mask, dtype=torch.long).cumsum(dim=1) - 1
    reversed_positions = lengths.unsqueeze(1) - 1 - positions
    source_positions = torch.where(
        positions < lengths.unsqueeze(1),
        reversed_positions,
        positions,
    ).clamp_min(0)
    return x.gather(1, source_positions.unsqueeze(-1).expand_as(x))


class ManualBidirectionalLstm(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.forward_rnn = torch.nn.LSTM(
            input_size=16,
            hidden_size=8,
            num_layers=1,
            batch_first=True,
            bidirectional=False,
            dropout=0.0,
        )
        self.backward_rnn = torch.nn.LSTM(
            input_size=16,
            hidden_size=8,
            num_layers=1,
            batch_first=True,
            bidirectional=False,
            dropout=0.0,
        )
        self.output = torch.nn.Linear(16, 16)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, key_padding_mask: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        forward, _ = self.forward_rnn(x)
        backward_input = reverse_valid_prefix(x, key_padding_mask)
        backward_reversed, _ = self.backward_rnn(backward_input)
        backward = reverse_valid_prefix(backward_reversed, key_padding_mask)
        return self.output(torch.cat((forward, backward), dim=-1))


def export_model(path: Path, *, dynamo: bool) -> None:
    model = ManualBidirectionalLstm().eval()
    x = torch.randn((1, 6, 16), dtype=torch.float32)
    key_padding_mask = torch.zeros((1, 6), dtype=torch.bool)

    kwargs = {
        "dynamo": dynamo,
        "external_data": False,
        "input_names": ["x", "key_padding_mask"],
        "output_names": ["y"],
        "opset_version": 18,
    }
    if dynamo:
        kwargs["dynamic_shapes"] = {
            "x": {0: torch.export.Dim.AUTO, 1: torch.export.Dim.AUTO},
            "key_padding_mask": {0: torch.export.Dim.AUTO, 1: torch.export.Dim.AUTO},
        }
    else:
        kwargs["dynamic_axes"] = {
            "x": {0: "batch", 1: "time"},
            "key_padding_mask": {0: "batch", 1: "time"},
            "y": {0: "batch", 1: "time"},
        }

    with redirect_stdout(StringIO()), redirect_stderr(StringIO()):
        torch.onnx.export(model, (x, key_padding_mask), path, **kwargs)


def run_onnx(path: Path, *, n_frames: int) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    session_options = ort.SessionOptions()
    session_options.log_severity_level = 4
    session = ort.InferenceSession(
        path.as_posix(),
        sess_options=session_options,
        providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"],
    )
    feeds = {
        "x": np.random.randn(1, n_frames, 16).astype(np.float32),

The public input time axis accepts a different length in the working cases. In the failing manual bidirectional cases from the full reproducer, the ONNX graph still contains the literal `6` in an internal `Expand` shape:

```text

```

This makes the exported model invalid for a different time length, such as `[1, 9, 16]`.

### Expected behavior

If `dynamo=True` export succeeds with a dynamic time axis, the exported ONNX model should run with a different valid sequence length.

The manual bidirectional LSTM and GRU cases should behave like the passing cases:

- export from `[1, 6, 16]`
- run in ONNX Runtime with `[1, 6, 16]`
- run in ONNX Runtime with `[1, 9, 16]`

- two unidirectional `nn.LSTM` or `nn.GRU` modules
- `torch.gather` with a mask-derived reverse index
- `torch.cat`
- `torch.nn.Linear`

The bare RNN and masked unidirectional cases in the full reproducer also work with `dynamo=True`.

The failure is not ONNX Runtime rejecting the public input shape. ONNX Runtime accepts the dynamic public input, then fails inside the graph because a shape derived from the export example length is frozen into an internal `Expand`.

issues.author: atalman
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

The `torch==2.13.0+rocm7.2` wheel fails the `torch.compile` smoke test with
`RuntimeError: Can't detect vectorized ISA for CPU` when it is imported/run on
a **non-ROCm** image (e.g. `pytorch/almalinux-builder:cpu-main`), where
`torch.cuda.is_available()` is `False` and the compile check exercises the
CPU / Inductor path.

This looks like a regression:

- ✅ `torch==2.12.1+rocm7.2` runs the **same** smoke test on the same
  environment and succeeds — it prints `Picked CPU ISA VecAVX2 bit width 256`.
- ✅ `torch==2.13.0+rocm7.2` succeeds when run on the **ROCm** builder image

builder image to detect the CPU vectorized ISA, whereas 2.12.1 did not.

issues.title: [MPS] Compiled training is 4x slower than eager because layout optimization forces channels_last
issues.author: eyupcanakman
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Training a small conv net on MPS with torch.compile runs 4.5x slower than eager on the current nightly, and 9x slower on the 2.13.0 release wheel.
There are zero graph breaks.
The cause is inductor's layout optimization, and setting `TORCHINDUCTOR_LAYOUT_OPTIMIZATION=0` turns compile into a win at every shape I tried.
I tracked it down with Claude's help and reviewed everything below.
The numbers are from my machine.

Repro, batch 256 at 32x32, bf16 autocast, Apple M5 Pro, macOS 27.

```python
import time
import torch
import torch.nn as nn


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c_in, c_out, stride=1):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 3, stride, 1, bias=False)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(c_out, c_out, 3, 1, 1, bias=False)
        self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out)
        self.short = (
            nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 1, stride, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out))
            if stride != 1 or c_in != c_out
            else nn.Identity()
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        out = torch.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x)))
        out = self.bn2(self.conv2(out))
        return torch.relu(out + self.short(x))


class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, w=24):
        super().__init__()
        self.stem = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(3, w, 3, 1, 1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(w), nn.ReLU())
        self.stage1 = Block(w, w)
        self.stage2 = nn.Sequential(Block(w, 2 * w, 2), Block(2 * w, 2 * w))
        self.stage3 = nn.Sequential(Block(2 * w, 4 * w, 2), Block(4 * w, 4 * w))
        self.head = nn.Linear(4 * w, 10)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.stage3(self.stage2(self.stage1(self.stem(x))))
        return self.head(x.mean(dim=(2, 3)))


dev = torch.device("mps")


def bench(compiled, iters=15):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    m = Net().to(dev)
    if compiled:
        m.compile()
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(m.parameters(), lr=0.1, momentum=0.9)
    lf = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    x = torch.randn(256, 3, 32, 32, device=dev)
    y = torch.randint(0, 10, (256,), device=dev)

    def step():
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        with torch.autocast("mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
            loss = lf(m(x), y)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()

    for i in range(iters + 5):
        if i == 5:
            torch.mps.synchronize()
            t = time.time()
        step()
    torch.mps.synchronize()
    return (time.time() - t) / iters * 1000


e = bench(False)
c = bench(True)
print(f"torch {torch.__version__}")
print(f"eager:    {e:7.2f} ms/step")
print(f"compiled: {c:7.2f} ms/step   ({c / e:.2f}x eager)")
```

Output.

```
torch 2.14.0.dev20260807
eager:      25.59 ms/step
compiled:  114.48 ms/step   (4.47x eager)
```

Same model swept across input shapes, eager -> compiled ms/step, with layout optimization on (default) and off (`TORCHINDUCTOR_LAYOUT_OPTIMIZATION=0`), each config in a fresh process and cache.

```
                 layout opt on (default)      TORCHINDUCTOR_LAYOUT_OPTIMIZATION=0
8x8   b256     7.20 ->   9.87   1.37x           7.18 ->  5.58   0.78x
16x16 b256     8.81 ->  31.65   3.59x           7.96 ->  6.75   0.85x
24x24 b128     8.46 ->  35.19   4.16x           8.42 ->  7.11   0.84x
32x32 b128    13.92 ->  60.50   4.35x          13.75 -> 11.95   0.87x
32x32 b256    27.36 -> 119.08   4.35x          27.38 -> 19.78   0.72x
```

With the flag, compiled is faster than eager at every shape.
The regression grows with spatial size, which matches the per-op numbers below.

AI-assisted analysis (Claude), reviewed by me:

`decide_layout_opt` in `torch/_inductor/graph.py` enables channels_last for graphs with convolutions, and `aten.convolution_backward` on MPS runs about 10x slower on channels_last inputs than on contiguous ones at common shapes, so the compiled backward pays that penalty 13 times per step.
With `backend="eager"` the step takes 27.0 ms and with `backend="aot_eager"` 26.5 ms, both matching eager, so the loss is inside inductor codegen rather than dynamo or AOTAutograd.
Timing every call in the generated backward code, with a sync around each call, attributes 84% of the backward to the 13 external `convolution_backward` calls at 8.3 ms per call, while no generated Metal kernel exceeds 1.3 ms.
The op on its own shows the layout penalty in bf16.

```
convolution_backward (256,24,32,32) w=(24,24,3,3)  contiguous 1.84 ms   channels_last 23.52 ms   12.8x
convolution_backward (256,48,16,16) w=(48,48,3,3)  contiguous 0.53 ms   channels_last  5.74 ms   10.9x
convolution_backward (256,96,8,8)   w=(96,96,5,5)  contiguous 1.92 ms   channels_last  3.86 ms    2.0x
```

Forward convolution is unaffected and is even faster on channels_last at these shapes (0.48 ms vs 0.94 ms at 32x32), so inference would not notice.

The heuristics in `decide_layout_opt` come from CUDA benchmarks (the code carries a `TODO - get different values per hardware`) and the function has no MPS branch.
The channels_last penalty inside MPS `convolution_backward` itself may deserve its own look, since it grows with spatial size.

End of the AI-assisted analysis.
I patched `decide_layout_opt` locally to skip layout optimization for MPS training graphs and compiled training went from 4.5x slower to 1.3x faster than eager.
I can send that patch if it is the right direction.

For reference, #150121 tracks compile on MPS but has no conv training performance item, and #189239 is the mirror problem on CUDA and XPU where backward graphs get too little channels_last rather than too much.

```

issues.title: [inductor] insert_overlap_deps wraps non-overlap-critical compute with control_deps, blocking fusion and causing silent bf16 accuracy regression
issues.author: lauri9
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch._inductor.config.aten_distributed_optimizations.insert_overlap_deps = True` (default since the overlap-scheduling pass landed) causes Inductor to emit strictly more, smaller Triton kernels for the *same* compute graph, by inserting `torch.ops.higher_order.control_deps` HOPs around compute that the overlap scheduler decides to reorder relative to a collective. The HOPs are no-ops at execution time, but Inductor's fuser treats them as opaque scheduling barriers and refuses to fuse `SchedulerNode`s across them. This is a fusion-quality regression that's silent in fp32 but produces real accuracy loss in bf16/fp16 inference.

### Reproducer
Standalone, vanilla PyTorch, two ranks, one collective + one fusion-candidate compute branch.

Run with: `torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node=2 repro.py`

```python
"""Minimal reproducer: insert_overlap_deps blocks Inductor SchedulerNode fusion."""
import os, sys
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.distributed._functional_collectives as funcol


class Model(torch.nn.Module):
    """Two parallel branches the overlap pass wants to schedule concurrently:
        branch A: all_to_all_single
        branch B: conv2d -> layer_norm -> +residual  (textbook fusion candidate)
    The merge at the bottom keeps both branches in one fx graph."""

    def __init__(self, c_in=64, c_out=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = torch.nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 3, padding=1)
        self.ln1  = torch.nn.LayerNorm(c_out)
        self.ln2  = torch.nn.LayerNorm(c_out)

    def forward(self, x_a2a, y):
        a = funcol.all_to_all_single(x_a2a.contiguous(), None, None, group=dist.group.WORLD)
        h = self.conv(y).permute(0, 2, 3, 1).contiguous()
        h = self.ln1(h)
        h = h + h.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        return self.ln2(a.reshape(h.shape) + h)


def _install_counters(state):
    """Count Triton kernels Inductor emits AND control_deps HOPs the overlap pass inserts."""
    from torch._inductor import async_compile as ac
    from torch._inductor.fx_passes import overlap_scheduling as op

    orig_triton, orig_sched = ac.AsyncCompile.triton, op.schedule_overlap_bucketing

    def _wrap_triton(self, n, src, device_str="cuda"):
        state["kernels"] += 1
        return orig_triton(self, n, src, device_str=device_str)

    def _wrap_sched(gm, *a, **kw):
        ret = orig_sched(gm, *a, **kw)
        state["control_deps"] += sum(1 for n in gm.graph.nodes
                                     if "control_deps" in getattr(n.target, "__name__", str(n.target)))
        return ret

    ac.AsyncCompile.triton        = _wrap_triton
    op.schedule_overlap_bucketing = _wrap_sched


def _compile_with(insert_overlap_deps: bool):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    aten = torch._inductor.config.aten_distributed_optimizations
    aten.enable_overlap_scheduling = True
    aten.collective_bucketing      = True
    aten.insert_overlap_deps       = insert_overlap_deps
    aten.collective_estimator      = "benchmark"
    torch._inductor.config.reorder_for_compute_comm_overlap = False
    torch._inductor.config.reorder_for_compute_comm_overlap_passes = []
    torch._inductor.config.fx_graph_cache        = False
    torch._inductor.config.fx_graph_remote_cache = False
    torch._inductor.config.force_disable_caches  = True


def main() -> int:
    rank, world = int(os.environ.get("RANK", "0")), int(os.environ.get("WORLD_SIZE", "1"))
    if world < 2:
        print("[skip] need torchrun --nproc-per-node>=2"); return 2
    torch.cuda.set_device(rank % torch.cuda.device_count())
    dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl")
    device = torch.device(f"cuda:{torch.cuda.current_device()}")

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = Model().to(device).eval()
    x_a2a = torch.randn(world * 64, 128 * 8, device=device)
    y     = torch.randn(1, 64, 32, 32,      device=device)

    state = {"kernels": 0, "control_deps": 0}
    _install_counters(state)

    def _run(flag: bool):
        state["kernels"] = 0; state["control_deps"] = 0
        _compile_with(flag)
        with torch.no_grad():
            out = torch.compile(model, dynamic=False)(x_a2a, y)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        return out, state["kernels"], state["control_deps"]

    out_off, n_off, cd_off = _run(False)
    out_on,  n_on,  cd_on  = _run(True)

    rc = 0
    if rank == 0:
        d = (out_off - out_on).abs().max().item()
        print(f"  insert_overlap_deps=False -> {n_off} Triton kernels, {cd_off} control_deps HOPs inserted")
        print(f"  insert_overlap_deps=True  -> {n_on } Triton kernels, {cd_on } control_deps HOPs inserted")
        print(f"  numerical: max|OFF - ON| = {d:.3e}  (fp32; below noise floor)")
        print("PASS  regression reproduced" if n_on > n_off else "FAIL  regression NOT reproduced")
        rc = 0 if n_on > n_off else 1
    dist.destroy_process_group()
    return rc


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
```

### Observed output

NVIDIA B200, PyTorch `2.12.0a0+0291f960b6.nv26.04.48445190` (NGC nightly, CUDA 13.2), Triton `3.6.0+git5d72932fc5`, 2 ranks via `torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node=2`:

```
insert_overlap_deps=False -> 6 Triton kernels, 0 control_deps HOPs inserted
insert_overlap_deps=True  -> 8 Triton kernels, 4 control_deps HOPs inserted
numerical: max|OFF - ON| = 7.508e-05  (fp32; below noise floor)
PASS  regression reproduced
```

(Kernel counts are summed across both ranks: 3 unique kernels per rank with the flag OFF, 4 with the flag ON. The same regression was previously observed on AMD MI355X / PyTorch `2.11.0` with 1 vs. 3 unique kernels per rank — i.e. the bug is not vendor- or build-specific.)

The OFF case generates a single fused reduction kernel:

- `triton_per_fused_add_clone_convolution_mean_native_layer_norm_permute_view_2` - fuses the conv-epilogue NHWC-permute + LN1 mean/var reduction + LN1 normalize + residual `+ h.mean(...)` + LN2 input prep into one persistent reduction kernel.

With the flag ON, three separate kernels with the intermediates materialized to global memory between them:

- `triton_red_fused_clone_native_layer_norm_permute_1` (LN1 mean/var reduction → DRAM),
- `triton_poi_fused_clone_native_layer_norm_permute_2` (LN1 normalize, reads the reduction's output back from DRAM),
- `triton_red_fused_add_mean_native_layer_norm_view_3` (the `+ h.mean(...)` residual and LN2 mean/var reduction).

Plus a small change in the conv-prep kernels (2 `triton_poi_fused_convolution_{0,1}` weight/input layout kernels with the flag OFF vs. 1 `triton_poi_fused_convolution_0` with the flag ON), netting +1 unique Triton kernel (×2 ranks = +2 total) per `control_deps` boundary that crosses a fusion candidate. The 4 inserted `control_deps` HOPs are the necessary precondition: with them removed, the fuser is free to merge the entire conv-epilogue → LN1 → residual → LN2 chain.

The mechanism is graph-topology-driven, not data-driven: it reproduces on the smallest one-collective-plus-one-compute-branch graph, and the OFF-vs-ON numerical delta in fp32 is at or below the LayerNorm reduction noise floor, but the kernels Inductor selects under ON are strictly worse than under OFF.

### Production impact

The fp32 reproducer above only shows the *structural* break. However, a numerical issue is possible at low precision. Each broken fusion boundary materializes an intermediate to memory in the model's storage dtype (bf16/fp16), discarding the fp32 accumulator of the fused kernel. The per-boundary error is small (1–2 ULPs) but compounds:

- Diffusion-transformer inference (e.g. Wan2.2-style i2v: 40 transformer blocks × 40 denoising steps × multiple conv/LN/proj fusion boundaries per block) accumulates thousands of these losses.
- We measured this on a 1104×832 i2v video pipeline: with `insert_overlap_deps=True` (default), output PSNR vs. an eager reference dropped ~2 dB and produced visible artifacting; flipping the flag to `False` (or disabling the overlap pass entirely) restored the eager-equivalent output. `force_disable_caches=True` did not change this, ruling out cache poisoning.


### Related upstream issues found

A search through `pytorch/pytorch` issues and PRs didn't surface an exact match. Closest in spirit: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/178875 - a different HOP-as-fusion-barrier issue, similar shape, suggests the general problem of HOPs blocking fusion is recognized.

comments.body:
I can also see the issue on a h100 rig, on https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/commit/8145d630e811c9ec098a632d9ea7f4d52a2ea16e merged May 5th, 00:19 GMT+3. @eellison IIUC, this is even before https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/182419 was published.

While playing with @lauri9 's reproducer, I noticed that it's very non-deterministic; up to a point that even setting an environment variable in command line to the same value it already has in the environment, changes the counter number of kernels in a range between 3 and 6. I investigated that and it turns out the reproducer has several sources of non-determinism, one of the most annoying/unexpected of which is a pool warmup race in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/8145d630e811c9ec098a632d9ea7f4d52a2ea16e/torch/_inductor/codegen/triton.py#L6579 . Whether it fires depends on whether implementation's `_ready_future.done()` at the moment each kernel is codegen'd. The first compile in a process is usually cold (produce fewer/no double counts); later compiles are warm (always doubles). So I slightly modified the repro to make it (to the best of my knowledge) deterministic by collecting a set of kernels used and looking for LayerNorm fusion pattern:

```py
"""Deterministic reproducer: insert_overlap_deps blocks Inductor LayerNorm fusion.
run as:
    torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node=2 repro2.py

The regression signal (environment-independent):
    insert_overlap_deps=False -> LayerNorm fuses into ONE persistent-reduction kernel
                                 (triton_per_fused_*native_layer_norm*)
    insert_overlap_deps=True  -> LayerNorm SPLITS into TWO reduction kernels
                                 (triton_red_fused_*native_layer_norm*)
    => regression reproduced iff #layernorm_kernels(ON) > #layernorm_kernels(OFF).

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/186084
"""

import os, re, sys
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.distributed._functional_collectives as funcol


class Model(torch.nn.Module):
    """Two parallel branches the overlap pass wants to schedule concurrently:
        branch A: all_to_all_single
        branch B: conv2d -> layer_norm -> +residual  (textbook fusion candidate)
    The merge at the bottom keeps both branches in one fx graph."""

    def __init__(self, c_in=64, c_out=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = torch.nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 3, padding=1)
        self.ln1  = torch.nn.LayerNorm(c_out)
        self.ln2  = torch.nn.LayerNorm(c_out)

    def forward(self, x_a2a, y):
        a = funcol.all_to_all_single(x_a2a.contiguous(), None, None, group=dist.group.WORLD)
        h = self.conv(y).permute(0, 2, 3, 1).contiguous()
        h = self.ln1(h)
        h = h + h.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        return self.ln2(a.reshape(h.shape) + h)


_KERNEL_DEF_RE = re.compile(r"def (triton_[a-z]+_fused_\w+)\(")
_KERNEL_ANY_RE = re.compile(r"triton_[a-z]+_fused_\w+")


def _kernel_names_from_src(src: str) -> set[str]:
    """Extract the distinct Triton kernel name(s) defined in a compiled source."""
    names = set(_KERNEL_DEF_RE.findall(src))
    if not names:  # fallback: any reference to a triton_*_fused_* symbol
        names = set(_KERNEL_ANY_RE.findall(src))
    return names


def _install_counters(state):
    """Collect the SET of distinct Triton kernel names Inductor emits (dedup is what
    makes this immune to the parallel-compile double-submit), and count control_deps
    HOPs the overlap pass inserts."""
    from torch._inductor import async_compile as ac
    from torch._inductor.fx_passes import overlap_scheduling as op

    orig_triton, orig_sched = ac.AsyncCompile.triton, op.schedule_overlap_bucketing

    def _wrap_triton(self, n, src, device_str="cuda"):
        state["kernels"].update(_kernel_names_from_src(src))
        return orig_triton(self, n, src, device_str=device_str)

    def _wrap_sched(gm, *a, **kw):
        ret = orig_sched(gm, *a, **kw)
        state["control_deps"] += sum(1 for n in gm.graph.nodes
                                     if "control_deps" in getattr(n.target, "__name__", str(n.target)))
        return ret

    ac.AsyncCompile.triton        = _wrap_triton
    op.schedule_overlap_bucketing = _wrap_sched


def _compile_with(insert_overlap_deps: bool):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    aten = torch._inductor.config.aten_distributed_optimizations
    aten.enable_overlap_scheduling = True
    aten.collective_bucketing      = True
    aten.insert_overlap_deps       = insert_overlap_deps
    # Analytical estimators => scheduling decisions are deterministic (no GPU timing).
    aten.collective_estimator      = "analytical"
    aten.compute_estimator         = "analytical"

    torch._inductor.config.reorder_for_compute_comm_overlap = False
    torch._inductor.config.reorder_for_compute_comm_overlap_passes = []
    torch._inductor.config.fx_graph_cache        = False
    torch._inductor.config.fx_graph_remote_cache = False
    torch._inductor.config.force_disable_caches  = True


def _layernorm_kernels(names: set[str]) -> list[str]:
    return sorted(k for k in names if "native_layer_norm" in k)


def main() -> int:
    rank, world = int(os.environ.get("RANK", "0")), int(os.environ.get("WORLD_SIZE", "1"))
    if world < 2:
        print("[skip] need torchrun --nproc-per-node>=2"); return 2
    torch.cuda.set_device(rank % torch.cuda.device_count())
    dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl")
    device = torch.device(f"cuda:{torch.cuda.current_device()}")

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = Model().to(device).eval()
    x_a2a = torch.randn(world * 64, 128 * 8, device=device)
    y     = torch.randn(1, 64, 32, 32,      device=device)

    state = {"kernels": set(), "control_deps": 0}
    _install_counters(state)

    def _run(flag: bool):
        state["kernels"] = set(); state["control_deps"] = 0
        _compile_with(flag)
        with torch.no_grad():
            out = torch.compile(model, dynamic=False)(x_a2a, y)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        return out, set(state["kernels"]), state["control_deps"]

    out_off, k_off, cd_off = _run(False)
    out_on,  k_on,  cd_on  = _run(True)

    ln_off, ln_on = _layernorm_kernels(k_off), _layernorm_kernels(k_on)

    rc = 0
    if rank == 0:
        d = (out_off - out_on).abs().max().item()
        print(f"  insert_overlap_deps=False -> {len(k_off)} unique kernels, "
              f"{len(ln_off)} LayerNorm kernel(s), {cd_off} control_deps HOPs")        
        print("     Unique kernels are:")
        for k in sorted(k_off):
            print(f"        {k}{"  <--- LN" if k in ln_off else ""}")

        print(f"  insert_overlap_deps=True  -> {len(k_on)} unique kernels, "
              f"{len(ln_on)} LayerNorm kernel(s), {cd_on} control_deps HOPs")
        print("     Unique kernels are:")
        for k in sorted(k_on):
            print(f"        {k}{"  <--- LN" if k in ln_on else ""}")
        print(f"  numerical: max|OFF - ON| = {d:.3e}  (fp32; below noise floor)")

        reproduced = len(ln_on) > len(ln_off)
        print("PASS  regression reproduced (insert_overlap_deps splits the LayerNorm fusion)"
              if reproduced else
              "FAIL  regression NOT reproduced (LayerNorm fusion unchanged)")
        rc = 0 if reproduced else 1

    dist.destroy_process_group()
    return rc


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
```

comments.body:
@IvanKobzarev , that's super nice to hear!

I'd like to add a few more cents to the initial info posted. So, on my H100 rig:

- With the flag off, one persistent reduction `triton_per_fused_add_clone_convolution_mean_native_layer_norm_permute_view_2` fuses the whole `conv->LN1->residual->LN2` chain.
- With it on, the chain splits into two looped reductions `(triton_red_fused_*_1 + triton_red_fused_*_2)` with the LN1 output materialized to DRAM (hence the silent accuracy reduction).

This confirms the underlying phenomenon is real. However!

HOPs are NOT runtime no-ops on this machine. Captured generated call() show this for both cases:

- OFF: `start -> conv -> wait -> mega-kernel(LN1+residual+LN2)`. The collective overlaps `conv` only.
- ON: `start -> conv -> LN1 -> wait -> kernel(residual+LN2)`. The collective overlaps `conv + LN1`.

I.e. the ordering dependency pulls LN1 into the collective's hiding window. Removing it (or making the fuser ignore it) would restore the mega-fusion but delete the LN1 overlap — there can't be both, because a kernel fusing LN2 must consume the collective output and therefore run after the wait.

The fuser rejects `can_fuse_vertical(LN1, residual+LN2)` with the reason "intermediate nodes between node1 & node2". The wait on LN1 control dep makes LN1 an ancestor of the wait; the residual+LN2 group consumes the wait output, so the wait is topologically wedged between them, breaking the fuse.

The scheduler bookkeeping shows this is a bad cost/benefit (not a spurious wrap). The `all_to_all` is estimated at `0.139 ms`, `conv` at `0.021` ms, LN1 region at 0.0003 ms; after scheduling the collective is still ~84% exposed (exposed_time_ms=0.117, is_exposed=True). So LN1 legitimately gets grabbed as a hiding node. It just buys only ~0.3 µs of overlap while costing a persistent-reduction fusion.

So it seems that the reason for the observed behavior is that the scheduler weighs overlap gain but is blind to the fusion cost of the ordering dep it inserts. So, I'd say it's more a overlap-vs-fusion trade-off (btw, there is [/was in my commit] an existing test that intentionally asserts control_deps blocks fusion `test/inductor/test_control_deps.py`). So a correct fix seems to be essentially a **policy decision about when overlap is worth a broken fusion**, but that's not all.

A separate issue here is the **accuracy guarantee**: if the guaranteed behavior is the fused one (i.e. even low precision computations must be maintained with `fp32` accuracy), then either the fusing must not be broken (irrespective of the overlap considerations), or the split parts must be wrapped in an accuracy preserving code, and its costs must have due weight in the split/fuse decision.

issues.title: [inductor][cudagraphs] SIGSEGV when a buffer allocated inside the compiled region is passed back as a mutated input
issues.author: Hakureirm
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Under `mode="reduce-overhead"`, a buffer that is first allocated *inside* the compiled
region and then passed back in on later calls segfaults the process. There is no Python
traceback and no message.

**Minimal reproducer**

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

W = 64

class M(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.lin = nn.Linear(W, W)

    def forward(self, x, state=None):
        if state is None:                      # first allocated inside the traced region
            state = torch.zeros_like(x)
        state.copy_(state + self.lin(x))       # ... mutated in place on later calls
        return x + state, state

c = torch.compile(M().cuda().eval(), mode="reduce-overhead")
x = torch.randn(1, W, device="cuda")

with torch.no_grad():
    out, state = c(x)                          # state=None
    for _ in range(5):
        out, state = c(torch.randn(1, W, device="cuda"), state)
```

It dies on the second call.

**Ablation**

- `mode="reduce-overhead"`: segfault. `mode="default"`: runs fine. So this is specific
  to cudagraphs.
- `torch.compiler.cudagraph_mark_step_begin()` before each call: no change, still a
  segfault.
- Allocating the buffer *before* `torch.compile` and passing it in: runs fine. That is
  the workaround we use.

**A check for this exists, but does not cover this path.** The same module fails in two
different ways depending only on what the caller passes:

| caller | result | message |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `c(out, state)` — feed the previous output back | `SIGABRT` | `accessing tensor output of CUDAGraphs that has been overwritten by a subsequent run` |
| `c(out.clone(), state)` — clone it first, as that message advises | **SIGSEGV** | none |
| `c(torch.randn(...), state)` — fresh input, carry only the state | **SIGSEGV** | none |
| `c(torch.randn(...))` — carry nothing | runs fine | — |

The last row is a control: drop the carried state and there is no crash, so the state
buffer is what the other three have in common.

The middle two rows are the ones I would flag. Following the advice in the existing
error message — "clone the tensor outside of `torch.compile()`" — turns a diagnosable
failure into a silent segfault, because the state buffer is still an unpinned allocation
from inside the traced region and nothing appears to check it.

**Where this came from.** A recurrent model, where the recurrent state is exactly such a
buffer: allocated on the first forward when the caller passes none, then handed back on
each decode step. A user who does not know to pre-allocate gets a segfault whose stack
contains nothing of their own code.

Reproduces identically on `2.13.0+cu130` and on nightly `2.14.0.dev20260809+cu130`.

The closest existing issues I found are #121861 (mutated inputs coming from a prior
cudagraph pool — closed, and describes skipping cudagraphs rather than crashing) and
#148439 (same error message from a different pattern — closed, and a `RuntimeError`
rather than a segfault). Neither reports a segfault, so this seemed worth filing
separately; happy to fold it into either if you would prefer.

### Error logs

There is no error output at all — the process dies with `Segmentation fault (core
dumped)`. Under `python -X faulthandler`:

```
Current thread (most recent call first):
  File "torch/_inductor/runtime/static_triton_launcher.py", line 309 in run

  File "torch/_inductor/cudagraph_trees.py", line 2519 in add_function
  File "torch/_inductor/cudagraph_trees.py", line 520 in cudagraphify
```

For contrast, the `c(out, state)` variant in the table above does produce output, from
`throw_data_ptr_access_error at c10/core/TensorImpl.cpp:356`:

The direct non-CUDA-Graph fallback can receive a CUDA Graph output whose storage has already been invalidated. Generated launchers may not perform the usual data pointer check before launching. Focused checks pass for the reported recurrent-state case, managed input mutation, forced rerecord fallback, wrapper tensors, Tensor subclasses, fake/meta inputs, generation cloning, inference, and grad mode. The check adds about 0.69 to 0.77 microseconds per concrete tensor only on direct fallback calls. Replay is unchanged.

Is this fix scope acceptable? If so, could the issue be marked `actionable`?

issues.title: torch.compile aborts if generated code contains an unhashable constant
issues.author: malfet
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Running
 ```python
 import torch


 @torch.compile
 def compiled(x):
     info = torch.iinfo(x.dtype)
     result = x + info.min // 2
     print(result)  # or torch._dynamo.graph_break()
     return torch.clamp_max(result, info.max - 3)


 print(compiled(torch.tensor([1, 2, 3], dtype=torch.int8)))
 ```

crashes with
 ```text
 libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type pybind11::error_already_set:
 TypeError: unhashable type: 'torch.iinfo'

 At:
   torch/_dynamo/bytecode_debugger.py(...): _dynamo_code_callback
   torch/_dynamo/eval_frame.py(...): compile_wrapper
 ```

### Codex Analysis
>
> Dynamo preserves the `torch.iinfo` value across the graph break and places it in the generated resume code object's `co_consts`. The bytecode debugger callback stores generated code objects in a set:
>
> ```python
> if code in self._tracked_codes:
>     return
> self._tracked_codes.add(code)
> ```
>
> Hashing a Python code object hashes its constants. Because `torch.iinfo` defines equality but is unhashable, hashing the generated code object raises `TypeError`.
>
> The Python exception escapes the C++ eval-frame callback boundary as `pybind11::error_already_set`, terminating the process instead of reporting a normal compilation error.
>
> A standalone demonstration of the underlying code-object behavior is:
>
> ```python
> import torch
>
>
> def f():
>     return 1
>
>
> code = f.__code__.replace(co_consts=(None, torch.iinfo(torch.int8)))
> print(hash(code))
> ```


### Versions

2.13.0/nightly
